explainer.subject: Chemistry
explainer.title: Resonance vs Inductive Effect in Anisole

steps.say: Looking at the -OCH3 group, oxygen is highly electronegative. It's natural to think it only pulls electrons away from the benzene ring via the inductive (-I) effect.
If the -I effect were dominant, anisole would be less reactive than benzene. In reality, anisole reacts much faster than benzene in electrophilic substitution.
The oxygen atom has lone pairs that are right next to the ring's pi system. These electrons can delocalize into the ring through overlapping p-orbitals.
This resonance (+R) effect pushes electron density into the ring, making it much more attractive to electrophiles (E+).
For groups with lone pairs on the joining atom (like -OH, -OR, -NH2), the +R effect is significantly stronger than the -I effect.
Therefore, even though oxygen is electronegative, -OCH3 is a strongly activating group that directs substitution to ortho and para positions.
Always check for lone pairs on the atom bonded to the ring. If a lone pair is present, think Resonance (+R) before Induction (-I).

explainer.takeaway: For oxygen and nitrogen groups, the electron-donating resonance effect is much stronger than their inductive withdrawal.
